entries.test: Public measurements of model performance gains relative to increases in training data and compute would show whether deep learning was experiencing diminishing returns by April 2025.
entries.note: The author explicitly defines the wall as diminishing results, rather than a complete halt in progress.
“GPT-5 level” supplies no shared capability threshold in this post. Comparing against a subsequently released product would impose a benchmark the author did not specify.
The claim concerns accomplishments as of publication. “GPT-5 level” lacks a defined or shared performance threshold.

entries.test: Public scaling experiments, Meta's disclosed training expenditures and performance targets, and Llama 4's measured results would test whether size alone predicted performance and whether substantial spending failed to deliver the intended gains.
entries.note: “Wasted” is evaluative, but the claim has a testable core about prediction sufficiency and unsuccessful expenditure.

entries.test: Contemporaneous surveys, reviews, and a representative sample of public reactions from AI researchers and practitioners would show whether disappointment with Llama 4 was widespread.
entries.note: This describes a broad community reaction, not unanimous disappointment.

entries.test: Public commentary by Roose, Newton, and Cowen before publication would show whether they addressed model-development setbacks, benchmark contamination, and implications for their AGI timelines.
entries.note: The surrounding paragraph gives concrete examples of the alleged omissions. “Alongside benchmark juicing” turns the source's conditional framing of that scandal into an unqualified premise.
This is an endorsed caution about standards of belief, rather than an empirical allegation that any particular company statement is false.

entries.test: Public customer surveys and a review of the named pundits' coverage would establish whether many customers were disappointed and whether real-world customers were rarely mentioned.
entries.note: The source says customers are rarely mentioned; the normalization instead says their disappointment is rarely mentioned.
“Appear to be” hedges the allegation of concealment. The compound claim combines a firm assertion about unmet expectations with a tentative allegation about vendor conduct.
